summary: Survey mainstream GPU device-side instrumentation scenarios and real workloads, classify their eBPF operations by direction, check what runs on the Orin

scenarios.name: S1 Kernel, block and warp entry/exit timing (block scheduling, tail effects, per-block duration)
scenarios.what_it_measures: Start clock, elapsed time and SM id of each warp or block in one launch. From these: block scheduling cost, tail effects, and per-block or per-thread finish timelines.
scenarios.who_uses_it: Neutrino block_sched (warp:array:16:1). It ran on torch.zeros and found about 20% of time spent scheduling 32,768 blocks (Neutrino §4.6), and a 24.69% tail effect in Triton FlashAttn-v2 and 50.93% in GEMM (§7, App. J). bpftime examples kernelretsnoop, kernel_trace and cuda-counter. gpu_ext kernelretsnoop on llama.cpp prefill: 8% overhead vs 85% for NVBit (arXiv 2512.12615v2 Table 2, WebFetch summary). KPerfIR, Proton and IKET record per-warp start/end too (see S7).
scenarios.typical_workloads: PyTorch elementwise kernels; Triton FlashAttention-v2; CUTLASS and Triton GEMM (Neutrino Table 3, §7). llama.cpp rope kernel in prefill: 4 x pp x 256 threads, so 524,288 threads per launch at pp512, 44 launches per run (gpu_ext runners via overlap survey).
scenarios.ebpf_operations: Expressible today. A kprobe (kernel entry) program and a kretprobe (kernel exit) program on the kernel. Helpers: 502 globaltimer, 503/505 blockIdx/threadIdx, 509 smid, 510 warpid, 511 laneid. The entry timestamp has to reach the exit program through a map, because they are separate programs. Neutrino keeps it in a probe register; this map need is [inferred] from bpftime's pass design. Today that means a per-thread array (1502), or a GPU array keyed by block or warp. At exit a GPU ringbuf (1527) record goes out per thread, or per warp-leader lane with a hand-written guard. Frequency: 2 probe firings per thread per launch, 1 record per warp (Neutrino) or per thread (bpftime kernelretsnoop).
scenarios.direction1_ops:
Yes, both state and output are thread-indexed today.
- Start timestamp: 8 B per thread in a 1502 map. At 524,288 threads that is 4 MiB [arithmetic].
- Output: 1527 ring with one ring per thread. gpu_ext's warp-sampled kernelretsnoop allocated 524,288 slots, 892 MiB, for 720,896 events (22 MiB). A pp32 run sized for 22,528 threads lost 450,560 events.
- With per-warp records: 524,288 / 32 = 16,384 warps x 44 launches = 720,896 records. At Neutrino's 16 B per record that is 11.5 MB per run [arithmetic].
- Neutrino avoids the guess by sizing grid x warps x 16 B at each launch.
scenarios.direction2_ops:
No mainstream tool does a host call per event.
- Neutrino copies its maps back after the kernel (cuda.c, App. C).
- bpftime cuda-counter keeps start_ts/total_time in CPU HASH maps and calls printk on entry and exit. That is host calls per thread per launch; the callsite survey classes them eliminate and defer.
- Cost of a naive port [inferred arithmetic at about 10 us per call]: one host call per thread at 524,288 threads is about 5.2 s per launch. Per warp leader it is 16,384 calls, about 0.16 s. Per launch (thread 0 only) it is about 10 us.
sources: https://open-neutrino.github.io/Neutrino-Preprint.pdf §3.3, §4.6, Fig. 10, Table 3, §7 Fig. 14, App. C, App. J

scenarios.name: S2 Kernel launch latency (host enqueue to device start)
scenarios.what_it_measures: Time from the host's cudaLaunchKernel (or launch stub) to the first instruction of the kernel on the GPU, per launch.
scenarios.who_uses_it: bpftime launchlate and launchlate-kernel-gpu-shared-map examples. gpu_ext launchlate on llama.cpp prefill: 14% overhead vs 93% for NVBit (arXiv 2512.12615v2 Table 2, WebFetch summary). Host-side timelines (Nsight Systems) give a similar answer from hardware timestamps without instrumentation [inferred].
scenarios.ebpf_operations:
Expressible today.
- A CPU uprobe on cudaLaunchKernel writes a calibrated host timestamp into a map.
- A GPU kprobe in thread 0 of block 0 reads that value, computes globaltimer minus timestamp, and adds to a histogram bucket.
- gpu_ext's version uses a 1513 FIFO with cursors.
- Frequency: one read and one histogram add per launch, by one thread.
scenarios.direction1_ops: None: state is per launch, not per thread.
scenarios.direction2_ops:
Small today.
- In the bpftime example, the GPU read of the CPU-written timestamp (ARRAY) and the histogram update (1503) are already GPU-local, with no host call (callsite survey: gpu_local_already).
- The remaining host calls are 2 printk per launch, classed defer.
- The CPU writes the value before the launch, so no synchronous round trip is needed.
- Volume: about 1-3 operations per launch, by one thread [inferred].

scenarios.name: S3 Work distribution and load imbalance (per-thread histogram, SM/warp mapping)
scenarios.what_it_measures: How many times each thread ran or exited, and which SM, warp and lane each thread landed on; per-SM and per-warp histograms of work.
scenarios.who_uses_it:
bpftime examples:
- threadhist on llama.cpp rms_norm_f32, PyTorch bitonicSortKVInPlace and faiss l2NormRowMajor.
- threadscheduling and threadscheduling_dynamic_hook.
- threadhist-gpu-kernel-shared-map.

gpu_ext:
- threadhist: 3% overhead vs NVBit 87% (arXiv Table 2).
- The paper's Fig. 2 shows a 127x SM imbalance (WebFetch summary).

Neutrino's block_sched records the SM id (cuid) per warp.
scenarios.typical_workloads: llama.cpp, PyTorch sort, faiss (bpftime examples); llama.cpp rope in gpu_ext.
scenarios.ebpf_operations:
Expressible today.
- A kretprobe increments a per-thread counter in a 1502 array, which the loader reads as a histogram.
- Alternatively, helpers 509/510/511 key per-SM or per-warp counters in a 1503 array with atomic add.
- threadscheduling uses CPU HASH maps.
- Frequency: 1 update per thread per launch.
scenarios.direction1_ops: Yes for the per-thread form: 8 B per thread, sized by a guessed count. gpu_ext's threadhist had 1,048,576 slots (8 MiB) with 22,528 used (2.1%). A histogram keyed by SM or warp id is sized by hardware, not by threads.
scenarios.direction2_ops: threadscheduling does CPU HASH updates per thread per launch: host calls. The survey classes them defer, and they aggregate per warp. A naive per-thread host call at 524,288 threads costs about 5.2 s per launch [inferred arithmetic].

scenarios.name: S4 Memory-access counts and bytes (global bytes, memory instructions, coalescing/cache lines per warp access)
scenarios.what_it_measures:
Per kernel or per thread:
- Number of global memory instructions.
- Bytes moved by synchronous (ld/st.global) and asynchronous (cp.async) accesses.
- Unique cache lines per warp-level access (coalescing).
scenarios.who_uses_it:
- Neutrino gmem_bytes (thread:array:8:1): 0.98x-1.39x slowdown (Table 3), checked against Nsight Compute (§6.1).
- NVBit MICRO'19 §6.1, Listing 8 (address divergence): run on Torch7 AlexNet, ENet, GoogLeNet, ResNet, VGG.
- Nsight Compute sass_ metrics, collected by SW patching (Profiling Guide §2.3.2).
- bpftime mem_trace example: counts __memcapture firings.
scenarios.typical_workloads:
Neutrino Table 3:
- CUTLASS GEMM and Conv2D.
- Triton FlashAttn-v2.
- PyTorch LayerNorm, Softmax, Pooling, Embedding.

NVBit: CNN training/inference using cuBLAS/cuDNN.
scenarios.direction1_ops:
Yes in bpftime: one per-thread accumulator slot (1502), updated per memory instruction per thread. Neutrino needs only 8 B per thread per launch, in a grid-sized map allocated at launch.

Volume [inferred arithmetic]:
- Memory instructions are 11.03% (attention) and 17.57% (GEMM) of executed instructions (Neutrino App. I).
- Assuming (not measured) an LLM decode step that streams a ~0.8 GB quantized 1B model once per token with 16-B per-thread loads: about 50 M thread-level loads (1.56 M warp-level) per token.
scenarios.direction2_ops: None in any tool surveyed. A naive port to a CPU map would make about 50 M host calls per token under the same assumption, about 500 s at 10 us each [inferred arithmetic]: infeasible. These counters aggregate per warp: NVBit has the first active lane do one atomicAdd per warp.

scenarios.name: S5 Memory address trace and access timeline (mem_trace, DMAT, cache/UVM simulation, page-access patterns)
scenarios.what_it_measures:
Every (or sampled) memory access with its address, often with a timestamp, thread/warp coordinates and opcode. Used for:
- Access-pattern plots (DMAT).
- Cache and memory simulation.
- Simulator traces.
- Page/UVM access patterns for prefetch and eviction.
scenarios.who_uses_it:
- NVBit mem_trace: one 288-B record per warp per memory instruction, 32 addresses, pushed to a channel.
- Neutrino dmat (thread:array:16:dynamic; ld.global, st.global, cp.async): 2.75x-13.16x slowdown, 7.12x average (Table 3, App. I). Used to compare attention algorithms (Fig. 11). Fig. 12 reports its probe-memory footprint, relative to model memory, over whole forward passes of ResNet, Stable Diffusion, Mamba-1.7B and Llama3-1/3/8B.
- eGPU HCDS'25 §6.1: ld/st hooks recording address, size and timestamp; evaluated only on a micro-benchmark (§7, WebFetch summary).
- CUTracer mem_addr_trace, mem_value_trace and tma_trace (Meta, NVBit-based).
- GVProf/DrGPUM GPU Patch (Compute Sanitizer based) records memory accesses into a GPU buffer.
- gpu_ext Fig. 1 page-fault patterns for faiss, llama.cpp MoE and PyTorch (tool unnamed, WebFetch summary).
scenarios.typical_workloads:
- FlashAttention v1/v2 and memory-efficient attention (Neutrino Fig. 11).
- Llama3 and Stable Diffusion forward passes (Neutrino Fig. 12, memory footprint only).
- Triton and PyTorch kernels (CUTracer).
- PyTorch models (DrGPUM, PASTA; search-level only).
scenarios.ebpf_operations:
Not expressible today: the __memcapture probe gets no address. It needs a pass change that passes the effective address (and width) as an argument, plus coverage of vector, shared and cp.async forms.

Once available:
- One 1527 ringbuf output per access per thread: 16 B with clock and address, like Neutrino.
- Or a warp-aggregated record of 32 addresses written by the leader lane, like NVBit.
- Frequency: per memory instruction per thread.
scenarios.direction1_ops:
Dominant. Storage grows as threads x accesses per thread, and the count is not known in advance.
- Neutrino runs the kernel once with a counting probe to get cap. Its source notes this breaks for kernels that modify inputs in place (cuda.c:486-493).
- NVBit uses one shared channel buffer reserved by atomicAdd, not per thread.

Volume for one LLM decode token [inferred arithmetic]. Same unmeasured assumptions as S4: ~0.8 GB of weights streamed per token, 16-B loads.
- 50 M thread-level accesses x 16 B is about 800 MB per token (Neutrino layout).
- 1.56 M warp-level accesses x 288 B is about 450 MB per token (NVBit layout).
scenarios.direction2_ops: No per-event host call in any tool read. NVBit's channel blocks only when the buffer is full: one warp waits for writers, rings a doorbell in host-mapped memory, and spins until the host thread drains it. That is one round trip per buffer fill (MBs), not per record. GPU Patch likewise signals the runtime when its GPU buffer (default 16 x 1024 records) is full.
sources: https://github.com/facebookexperimental/CUTracer/blob/main/README.md (trace modes; WebFetch summary, hang section read raw)

scenarios.name: S6 Instruction mix: instruction counts, opcode histograms, tensor-op counts
scenarios.what_it_measures: Dynamic instruction counts per kernel, per opcode or per PC; thread-level vs warp-level instruction counts (divergence efficiency); number of tensor-core mma instructions.
scenarios.who_uses_it:
- NVBit instr_count, instr_count_bb and opcode_hist (first active lane does one atomicAdd per warp). The MICRO'19 §6.2 top-5 histogram on SpecAccel ran 36.4x slower on average (up to 112x) when fully instrumented, and 2.3x with per-grid-shape kernel sampling (<0.6% error).
- Neutrino tensorop_count (mma.sync.aligned; thread:array:8:1).
- Nsight Compute InstructionStats and sass_* metrics (SW patching, separate replay passes, highest overhead).
- CUPTI SASS Metrics API: per-instruction counters per GPU/SM/SMSP instance (search-level).
- CUTracer opcode_only and proton_instr_histogram.
scenarios.typical_workloads: SpecAccel (NVBit); CUTLASS/Triton/PyTorch kernels (Neutrino Table 3); Triton kernels (CUTracer). NVBit §6.1 found 74-96% (average 88%) of the instructions executed by CNN workloads were inside precompiled libraries (cuBLAS/cuDNN).
scenarios.ebpf_operations:
Not expressible today: bpftime's PTX passes give kernel entry, kernel exit and __memcapture only, with no per-instruction or opcode-selected attach point. A new pass would insert a call before chosen PTX instructions (all, or a class such as mma).

The operation would then be:
- One atomic add per warp-instruction into a counter keyed by opcode or PC (1503 array).
- Or a per-thread register-style counter saved once at exit.
- Frequency: every executed instruction per warp, the highest-frequency scenario.
scenarios.direction1_ops: Not needed when counters are keyed by opcode or PC (sized by code, not threads). Neutrino's tensorop_count does save one 8-B value per thread (grid-sized map at launch). In bpftime, a per-thread accumulator would again need a 1502 slot updated per instruction [inferred].
scenarios.direction2_ops: None in any tool; counters live on the GPU and are read after the kernel.

scenarios.name: S7 Intra-kernel region and progress timing (per-warp region timers, branch-sampled progress, pipeline stages)
scenarios.what_it_measures:
Per warp or warp group: timestamps at region boundaries or loop back-edges inside the kernel. Used for:
- Pipeline bubbles.
- Producer/consumer overlap in warp-specialized GEMM and attention.
- Per-block throughput over time.
scenarios.who_uses_it:
- Neutrino program_progress: bra probe, thread:array:8:128. Used in §7 to find the slow-then-fast stage in shared-block FlashAttn-v2.
- KPerfIR (OSDI'25, Triton/Proton): 8-B records in a circular buffer per warp group in shared memory, about 8% overhead (§5.2, §6.3). It was used to speed up FA3 on H100 by 24.1% (WebFetch summary).
- Proton instrumentation mode: proton_gpu.circular_store drops older counters when a segment is full.
- NVIDIA CUTLASS CuTe DSL IKET: per-warp events, an estimation pass, then allocation with margin and --max-ts-cnt-per-warp.
- Triton-distributed intra-kernel profiler: max_num_profile_slots must exceed total records, as the user's responsibility.
- FlashInfer intra-kernel profiler (PR #913; search-level only).
scenarios.typical_workloads: FlashAttention-2/3 and GEMM on A100/H100/MI300X (Neutrino §7, KPerfIR §6); LLM serving kernels (FlashInfer, Triton-distributed; not checked in detail).
scenarios.ebpf_operations:
Not expressible today. It needs an attach point at a chosen PTX instruction (bra, a marker, a line-info range), the way Neutrino's tracepoints work. After that, the per-event operation is:
- globaltimer, warpid, smid.
- One append by the warp leader into a per-warp buffer.
- Frequency: per loop iteration or region boundary per warp, typically tens to hundreds per warp per launch (Neutrino cap 128 per thread).
scenarios.direction1_ops:
Yes: a per-warp (or per-thread) buffer whose capacity is guessed. The mainstream answers are:
- Overwrite the oldest records (KPerfIR, Proton).
- A sizing pre-pass (IKET).
- A fixed cap (Neutrino 128).
- User sizing (Triton-distributed).

IKET's docs warn that a record-count mismatch between passes can give wrong data or an illegal memory access.
scenarios.direction2_ops: None; buffers are copied after the kernel (KPerfIR §4.3: managed memory or a high-priority copy stream).

scenarios.name: S8 Value and correctness checking (register values, NaN/Inf, out-of-bounds, races, uninitialized reads, barrier misuse, hangs)
scenarios.what_it_measures: Register or loaded values at chosen instructions (e.g. where NaN/Inf first appears), floating-point exceptions, memory-safety errors, shared-memory races, uninitialized reads, barrier misuse, and hung warps.
scenarios.who_uses_it:
- NVBit record_reg_vals: a 1,048-B reg_info_t per warp per instrumented instruction.
- GPU-FPX (LLNL, NVBit-based, HPDC'23; search-level).
- Compute Sanitizer memcheck, racecheck, initcheck and synccheck. Racecheck caps hazards with NV_COMPUTE_SANITIZER_MAX_RACECHECK_HAZARDS (default 10,000,000).
- The Sanitizer patch API lists the device events such tools hook: global/shared/local memory access, barriers, syncwarp, shfl, call/ret, device malloc/free, matrix memory access, bulk copies, warpgroup MMA (sanitizer_patching.h:799-1028).
- CUTracer: reg_trace, mem_value_trace, deadlock_detection and random_delay race search.
- DrGPUM and ValueExpert (Sanitizer-based value and memory-inefficiency profilers on PyTorch models; search-level).
scenarios.typical_workloads: Debugging training/inference numerics and new hand-written kernels (Triton, TorchInductor, CUTLASS) rather than always-on production [inferred from CUTracer and Sanitizer docs].
scenarios.ebpf_operations:
Mostly not expressible today:
- No per-instruction attach.
- The memcapture context gives no address or register values.

A memcheck-style check would need, per memory access per thread, the address plus a read-only lookup in an allocation-range table kept by CPU uprobes on cudaMalloc/cudaFree [inferred]. An error report would be one rare ringbuf record.
scenarios.direction1_ops: Shadow state is sized by allocations or shared memory, not by thread count [inferred]. Error buffers are small and shared. A per-thread value trace (record_reg_vals style) would be thread x instruction sized like S5.
scenarios.direction2_ops:
Error reports are rare: one per error (Sanitizer prints the first 100 by default, --print-limit). The allocation table is CPU-written and read-mostly, so it can be mirrored to the GPU before launch with no synchronous call [inferred].

The one mainstream case of per-record synchronous delivery is here: CUTracer's hang debugging. It runs deadlock_detection with --channel-records 1, which 'flushes every record, so the trace reaches the moment of the hang'. A hung kernel never reaches a post-kernel copy or a buffer-full flush, so deferred output would be lost. With NVBit's channel, a one-record buffer means every push waits for the host to drain [inferred from channel.hpp]. Debugging hangs and crashes is therefore the use case where deferral does not work.

scenarios.name: S9 Device-side printing and logging (bpf_printk, puts, mem_printf)
scenarios.what_it_measures: Free-form messages from probes: debug output, per-thread event lines.
scenarios.who_uses_it:
- bpftime examples: 21 of the 59 host-call sites are printk or puts, output only.
- NVBit mem_printf2 pushes a formatted message per access into the channel.
- CUDA device printf: buffered in a fixed-size FIFO (1 MB default) and flushed at sync points (search-level).
scenarios.typical_workloads: Tool development and debugging; bpftime examples run them per thread per launch on vectorAdd, CUTLASS, llama.cpp test kernels.
scenarios.ebpf_operations: Expressible today. bpf_trace_printk and helper 501 (puts) each make a host_call: the request goes to a CPU thread and the probe waits for the response. Frequency in the examples: per thread per launch (49 of the 59 host-call sites are per thread per launch).
scenarios.direction1_ops: None, or a shared log buffer.
scenarios.direction2_ops: Every call is a synchronous round trip today, about 8.7-10.2 us per call on the Orin with lanes serialized. No caller uses the return value: the survey classes them defer, with an ordering caveat. Mainstream practice (CUDA printf, NVBit channel) buffers on the GPU and drains later. The caveat is that deferred output is lost if the kernel hangs or crashes before the drain; CUTracer's --channel-records 1 exists for that case (S8).

scenarios.what_it_measures:
Not measurement: probes change behavior.
- Skip or partition blocks.
- Decide work stealing in persistent kernels.
- Issue L2 prefetch.
- Ask the host driver to prefetch UVM regions.
scenarios.who_uses_it:
bpftime atomizer: blocks read a CPU-written partition from a 1503 array and exit via bpf_cuda_exit (helper 507).

gpu_ext (arXiv 2512.12615v2, WebFetch summary):
- Work-stealing block scheduler (should_try_steal; §4.3.2, §6.2.1).
- Device-side L2 stride prefetch: 1.34x, or 1.77x combined with the host (§6.2.1, Table 1).

scenarios.ebpf_operations:
Partly expressible today:
- Entry probe plus a 1503 read plus bpf_cuda_exit (atomizer).
- Per-block or per-warp decisions on GPU maps.
- A device-to-host prefetch request would be a helper with no answer needed.
scenarios.direction1_ops: Per-warp or per-SM shards for access counters: gpu_ext §5.3 describes warp-aggregated counters written to GPU-local map shards.
scenarios.direction2_ops: gdev_mem_prefetch-style requests: one per predicted region per warp. They are asynchronous by nature, since the probe does not wait for the prefetch [inferred]. CPU-written configuration is read per block and is already GPU-local (1503).

findings.claim: bpftime's GPU attach points are kernel entry (kprobe), kernel exit (kretprobe) and kprobe/__memcapture only. There is no attach point at an arbitrary or opcode-selected instruction, so S6, S7 and most of S8 need a new PTX pass.

__memcapture hands the eBPF program a pointer to the instruction's PTX text on the eBPF stack, not the effective address. Address traces (S5) and coalescing analysis (S4) cannot be written today.

Its regex matches only ld/st with an explicit const/global/local/param state space and a scalar type. Tested with python3 -I on sample lines:
- ld.global.u32 and ld.param.u64 match.
- These do not: generic ld.u32, ld.shared.f32, ld.global.nc.f32, ld.global.v4.u32.
- cp.async and atomics are outside the pattern.

The regex misses generic, vector, .nc and cp.async loads, which LLM GEMV/GEMM/attention kernels use for most of their traffic. So memcapture probably sees only a small part of the memory traffic of real LLM kernels. Not checked by compiling llama.cpp kernels.
findings.source: main.cpp:45-46 regex vs Neutrino preprint §2 (memory access in PTX is ld, st, cp.async and tensormap)

findings.claim: Per-thread GPU maps index by a linear global thread id. A thread past max_thread_count gets NULL from a 1502 lookup, with one warning print per module, and 1 from a 1527 output (dropped silently).

On this Orin (sm_87), the installed cuBLAS 13.4, cuBLASLt and cuDNN 9.20 libraries carry PTX only for sm_120/sm_121, plus one sm_75 PTX entry in cuBLASLt. Their code is otherwise SASS for sm_75/80/86/89/90/100/110/120 etc.:
- libcublas: 1260 ELF and 188 PTX entries, all PTX sm_120.
- libcublasLt: 6275 ELF; PTX 289 sm_120 + 1 sm_75.
- libcudnn_engines_precompiled: 4980 ELF; 93 PTX sm_121.
- libcudnn_ops, adv and cnn: PTX sm_121 only.
Counts are fatbin entries, not kernels. The --list-ptx output names the entries <lib>.N.sm_120.ptx.

bpftime therefore probably cannot instrument cuBLAS/cuDNN GEMM, attention and conv kernels on the board. It extracts PTX with cuobjdump --extract-ptx, and pick_patched_ptx skips PTX whose file name carries an SM newer than the device. When nothing is left the kernels run unpatched, and a fatbin with no PTX gets a warning. This is deduced from the code and the listing, not run against cuBLAS. It also assumes the extract names match the --list-ptx names.

NVBit measured that 74-96% (average 88%) of the instructions executed by Torch7 CNN workloads (AlexNet, ENet, GoogLeNet, ResNet, VGG) ran inside precompiled cuBLAS/cuDNN. Excluding them distorted the memory-divergence result. Together with the cuBLAS/cuDNN finding above, much of a real DL workload's device work is outside what PTX patching can reach on this board. The 88% figure is from 2019-era CNNs, not today's LLM stacks.

Neutrino sizes its maps at every launch from the launch configuration. A thread map is grid x block x cap x size and a warp map is grid x warps x cap x size. For cap='dynamic' it first launches a counting copy of the kernel, copies the per-thread counts back (blocking) and uses the maximum. The source comments that this breaks for kernels that modify their inputs in place (e.g. top-p/top-k decode kernels). This is an external precedent for 'size at launch' that bpftime and gpu_ext lack.

Neutrino probes in one thread share probe registers. gmem_bytes and tensorop_count accumulate in a register and save one value per thread at kernel end. bpftime's programs are separate PTX functions with their own eBPF stacks, so the same tool needs a map read-modify-write per event.

findings.claim:
Neutrino overheads (Table 3, A100/RTX4090):
- Lightweight probes (block_sched, gmem_bytes, tensorop_count): about 1.04x on average.
- dmat: 2.75x (FlashAttn-v2) to 13.16x (SoftMax), 7.12x on average.
- Slowdown scales with sampling rate. Memory instructions are 11.03% (attention) and 17.57% (GEMM) of executed instructions (App. I).

NVBit's example tools aggregate per warp: the first active lane does one atomicAdd (instr_count, opcode_hist) or pushes one record holding all 32 lanes' values (mem_trace 288 B, record_reg_vals 1,048 B). The channel is one shared device buffer. Writers reserve space with atomicAdd; when it is full, one warp waits, rings a host-mapped doorbell and spins until the host thread drains it. Host involvement is per buffer fill, not per event.

findings.claim: NVBit's instruction-histogram tool slowed SpecAccel 36.4x on average (up to 112x) with full instrumentation. Instrumenting only one launch per unique grid shape cut this to 2.3x with under 0.6% error.

Of the tools whose device-to-host data path was read, none makes a synchronous round trip per event in normal use:
- Neutrino: blocking memcpy of its maps after the kernel.
- NVBit channel: one blocking flush per buffer fill.
- GVProf GPU Patch: signal when the GPU buffer is full, then copy.
- KPerfIR: copy back after the kernel, through managed memory or a high-priority stream.
The data path of Compute Sanitizer, IKET, Triton-distributed and Proton was not read.

The one documented per-record synchronous delivery is CUTracer's --channel-records 1, used to debug hangs: 'flushes every record, so the trace reaches the moment of the hang'.

Direction 2's synchronous helper path has a counterpart only in that debugging mode. Its everyday users are bpftime's own examples (59 sites, 0 needing a synchronous answer).

Fixed capacity guessed or measured in advance is the norm, and each tool handles overflow differently:
- KPerfIR: per-warp-group circular buffer in shared memory, oldest overwritten.
- Proton: circular_store drops older counters.
- IKET: estimation pass, then --max-ts-cnt-per-warp; a mismatch can give wrong data or an illegal memory access.
- Triton-distributed: user sizes max_num_profile_slots.
- GPU Patch: 16 x 1024 records by default.
- Compute Sanitizer: racecheck capped at 10 M hazards.
Direction 1's problem (capacity versus a workload-dependent number of records) is general, not bpftime-specific.

Real-workload geometry from gpu_ext's llama.cpp runs:
- The rope kernel launches 4 x pp x 256 threads: 32,768 at pp32 and 524,288 at pp512, 44 launches per run.
- The per-thread ring (1527) for warp-sampled kernelretsnoop took 892 MiB for 720,896 events (22 MiB).
- A pp32 run sized for 22,528 threads dropped 450,560 events, exactly (32,768 - 22,528) x 44.

gpu_ext arXiv v2 Table 2 (llama.cpp prefill, Llama 1B, P40): kernelretsnoop 8% vs NVBit 85%; threadhist 3% vs 87%; launchlate 14% vs 93%. These are whole-tool numbers with hand-written warp-uniform tools, not the later re-run rows in the gpu_ext repository.
Nsight Compute collects metrics with sass_ in the name by SW patching, in separate replay passes, and calls this the highest-overhead collection mode.

The Compute Sanitizer patch API exposes these device events: block enter/exit, global/shared/local/remote-shared memory access, barriers, syncwarp, shfl, call/ret, device malloc/free, memcpy_async and pipeline commit/wait, matrix memory access, warpgroup MMA, bulk (TMA) copies and reductions. This is the vendor's list of what sanitizers and Sanitizer-based profilers (GVProf, DrGPUM, PASTA) instrument.

eGPU (HCDS'25) hooks ld/st to capture address, size and timestamp per access for a GPU memory observer and CXL latency simulator. It evaluated only a load/store micro-benchmark on a P40 against NVBit; §7.2 says complex real-world workloads were not covered.

On the Orin, a bpftime host call costs 8.7-10.2 us per call in the dev branch for CPU map cases (32 calls per launch, one warp), and 15.6/10.4/9.9/9.8 us for 1 thread / 1 / 8 / 32 warps calling. Per-thread host calls on a 524,288-thread launch would cost seconds per launch [arithmetic].

bpftime's mem_trace example increments a 1503 counter with a non-atomic *val = *val + 1 from every thread at every matched ld/st. Concurrent lanes and warps can lose increments, the same class of bug as upstream #740.

Neutrino's hook driver documents an option to fall back to the real driver when the caller is cuBLAS ('filter out proprietary products like cublas for legal safety'). Neutrino's own evaluation also focuses on CUTLASS, Triton and PyTorch-native kernels rather than cuBLAS/cuDNN.

Host-side-only GPU observability is out of scope here: it times or counts CUDA API calls and memory events without running code in kernels. Examples: GPUprobe (eBPF uprobes on cudaMalloc/cudaFree/cudaLaunchKernel), Datadog agent pkg/gpu, PyTorch profiler/Kineto (CUPTI activity), Nsight Systems. Hardware-counter metrics and PC-sampling stall reasons (Nsight Compute; Neutrino Table 4) are not instrumentation and cannot be expressed as GPU eBPF.

The 59 host-call sites in bpftime's GPU examples are 21 printk, 20 maps only GPU probes touch, and 18 maps the CPU reads but the probe does not need back. 49 run per thread per launch and 51 are aggregatable per warp. gpu_ext's 15 device-side tools make no host calls; they were rewritten by hand around GPU map types.

gaps: No dynamic share was measured. For a real LLM run on the Orin, this survey gives no count of probe firings, map operations or records per scenario. The volumes above are arithmetic from published geometry (llama.cpp rope 524,288 threads x 44 launches; ~0.8 GB weights per decode token, which is an assumption) and published instruction shares (Neutrino App. I). The advisor's 'share in real applications' question needs a counting run, e.g. per-kernel instruction/memory-instruction counts with Nsight Compute sass_ metrics, or a bpftime entry/exit plus memcapture counting pass on llama.cpp.

No source gives the split of LLM inference GPU time between cuBLAS/cuDNN kernels (no usable PTX on sm_87) and framework kernels with PTX (llama.cpp ggml-cuda, PyTorch ATen, Triton) on Jetson. NVBit's 88% is 2019 Torch7 CNNs. llama.cpp, PyTorch and Triton binaries are not on the board, so their PTX coverage was not checked. Whether Triton-JITed cubins (loaded via cuModuleLoadData) are reachable by bpftime was not checked.

Several sources were read only through WebFetch's small-model summaries, so their wording is not verbatim: KPerfIR, Proton ops, IKET, Triton-distributed, Compute Sanitizer and Sanitizer API guide, Nsight Compute guide, eGPU, gpu_ext arXiv. Numbers taken from them should be re-checked against the PDFs before citing in a paper.

Search snippets only, not opened: GPU-FPX (16x faster than BinFPE, 151 programs), PASTA/AccelProf (up to 1.3e4x faster), CUPTI SASS Metrics API details, CUDA printf FIFO behavior, FlashInfer intra-kernel profiler PR #913, TVM CudaProfiler, GPUprobe, Datadog pkg/gpu.

Not covered: Accel-Sim tracer (NVBit traces for simulation), HPCToolkit GPU instrumentation, AMD Omniprobe/rocprofiler instrumentation, Intel GTPin tools, NCCL profiler plugin device events, ThunderKittens/megakernel timing instrumentation.
Neutrino Fig. 12 (probe memory vs model memory on Llama3-1/3/8B) and Fig. 13 values are only in the figures and were not extracted.

Production (always-on) in-kernel observability deployments were not found. Industry device-side tools found are developer tools (CUTracer, Proton/KPerfIR, IKET, FlashInfer and Triton-distributed profilers, Compute Sanitizer), used on LLM kernels during kernel development, not in serving. Whether anyone runs device-side probes continuously in production is unknown.

The memcapture regex coverage of real LLM kernels (which fraction of their ld/st PTX lines match) was not measured. It needs dumping PTX of llama.cpp kernels and counting matches, which is read-only but was not done here.

The data path of Compute Sanitizer, IKET, Triton-distributed and Proton (whether any of them ever blocks per record) was not read; the 'no per-event synchronous round trip' finding covers only Neutrino, NVBit, GVProf GPU Patch, KPerfIR and CUTracer.

added.claim:
The memcapture pass has further limits that matter for real kernels:
- It runs on the module's full PTX with no kernel selector, so it instruments every function in the fatbin.
- It emits the call after each matched instruction.
- It compiles a separate copy of the eBPF program per matched site (__memcapture__1..N), so code size grows with the number of ld/st lines.
- It never sees predicated (@%p) loads or cache-hinted forms (.ca, L1::evict_last).
- It does fire on ld.param and ld.local, which are not global traffic.

Kernel-time share on an sm_87 Jetson: in PyTorch/Transformers inference, GEMM is 76.0% of kernel time for Qwen-1.5B on Orin NX and 67.5% on AGX Orin; for Gemma-2B it is 44.8% on Orin NX. These GEMMs are cuBLAS calls in PyTorch [inferred], so 45-76% of GPU kernel time in PyTorch LLM inference on Orin falls in kernels bpftime cannot patch.

In llama.cpp the hot kernels are its own. On H100 (Llama-3.1-8B), Q4_K_M decode is 75.5% mul_mat_vec_q-family GPU kernel time and BF16 decode is 86.9% mul_mat_vec_f. Q4_K_M prefill is mul_mat_q plus fixup kernels; only BF16 prefill uses cuBLAS (sm90_xmma_gemm_bf16) plus flash_attn_ext_f16. The thesis states that its Orin kernel-level analysis is less detailed.

llama.cpp's MMQ rule: ggml_cuda_should_use_mmq returns false only under GGML_CUDA_FORCE_CUBLAS, an unsupported type, or less than 48 KiB shared memory per block. It returns true when turing_mma_available(cc). On the Orin (sm_87, at least Turing) quantized matmuls therefore run in llama.cpp's own MMQ kernels.

Real-application grid sizes for direction 1. The llama.cpp RoPE kernel (TinyLlama-1.1B) launches 4 x pp x 256 threads: 32,768 at pp32 and 524,288 threads (16,384 warps) at pp512, with 44 launches of that kernel per pp512 run. The grid therefore scales with prompt length (16x between pp32 and pp512), and one fixed thread count is either lossy or oversized.

Measured direction-1 symptoms in that real application. (a) A pp32 preflight sized for 22,528 threads dropped 450,560 events, exactly (32,768 - 22,528) x 44. (b) The July pp512 result used 8,192 slots for a 524,288-thread kernel. (c) The per-thread ring for 524,288 slots x 44 records is 935,329,824 B (about 892 MiB) for 720,896 x 32 B (about 22 MiB) of data. (d) threadhist defaults to 1,048,576 threads.

Direction-2 arithmetic on the one measured real-application geometry. The assumptions are one serialized host call per probe execution and our measured 9.7-14.2 us per call. One host call per thread per launch on RoPE at pp512 gives 524,288 x 44 = 23.1M calls, about 225-330 s per prefill. Per warp it gives 720,896 calls, about 7-10 s. Once per launch it gives 44 calls, about 0.4-0.6 ms. For comparison, 49 of the 59 host-call sites in bpftime's examples run once per thread per launch and 10 once per launch.

gpu_ext's real-application evaluation of device-side eBPF is one workload: llama.cpp prefill on one RoPE kernel with three tools and CUDA graphs disabled. The submitted P40 table gives 8/3/14% vs NVBit 85/87/93%; the paper text says '3-14% vs 85-87%', which disagrees with the 93% in the table. Its later RTX 5090 revision runs of the original kernelretsnoop lose 90.7-90.8% throughput. A hand-written GPU-local array gets 5.573%, and the transport-optimised original ring still loses about 99.5%. Its GPT-OSS-120B, vLLM, GNN, FAISS and HotSpot/K-Means results evaluate host-side driver policies.

findings.claim: bpftime dev's default load-substitution path chooses only PTX whose architecture is at or below the device's (pick_patched_ptx skips 'PTX for a newer GPU'). If none fits, it returns nullptr and the original image loads with no message ('no probed kernel in this fatbin'). Probes on cuBLAS/cuDNN kernels (sm_120/121 PTX only) would silently never fire on the Orin. That the load hook sees those libraries at all is untested.

cuBLAS, cuBLASLt, cuDNN and libnvinfer do not NEED libcudart.so (each embeds its own runtime). bpftime's cudart-level hooks (dlsym RTLD_NEXT __cudaRegisterFatBinary, exported cudaLaunchKernel) cannot see their fatbins; only the driver-level hooks (cuLibraryLoadData, cuLaunchKernel, graph node APIs) could.

sm_80/sm_86 SASS runs on the sm_87 Orin without JIT (NVIDIA: 'Orin can run sm_80 SASS code'), so vendor libraries and upstream PyTorch wheels run on this board with no sm_87 code at all. For PTX-level instrumentation this means running is not the same as attachable.

llama.cpp's default CUDA build is not attachable but a configured one is: GGML_NATIVE=ON by default gives CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=native, and nvcc -arch=native on this board emits sm_87 SASS only. With GGML_NATIVE=OFF the CUDA-13 list includes 75-virtual and 80-virtual (PTX that bpftime could pick); an explicit plain '87' generates both SASS and PTX. cudart is linked shared unless GGML_STATIC=ON. CUDA graphs are on by default (GGML_CUDA_GRAPHS_DEFAULT ON).

Kernel launch volume in framework LLM inference (PyTorch eager, H100, BF16, BS=4/SL=2048): Llama-3.2-1B dispatches 847.5 kernels per output token and Llama-3.2-3B 1,536.9. MoE models are 8-11x higher (OLMoE-1B/7B 9,305.3, Qwen1.5-MoE 6,695.1). The null-kernel launch floor is 4.7 us on H100. These are not llama.cpp numbers.

findings.claim: Scale of launches in realistic suites: MLPerf SSD training launches 5.3 million kernels. Rodinia inputs run under 1 ms on silicon. gaussian_208 has 414 kernels, gramschmidt 6,411 and fdtd2d 1,500.

Neutrino's per-kernel overhead on real kernels (CUTLASS GEMMs/Conv2D, Triton FA-v2/LayerNorm/Softmax, PyTorch pooling/embedding/gather): lightweight probes average 1.04x, while heavy memory tracing (dmat) averages 7.12x (mem_trace up to 13.2x on SoftMax). NVBit full instrumentation averages 36.4x on SPEC ACCEL, up to 112x.

FAISS splits work between vendor and own code. Brute-force search and the IVF coarse quantizer use a cuBLAS GEMM plus FAISS's own fused k-selection kernel; IVF list scanning is FAISS's own kernels, one block per (query, list) pair.

bpftime's own real-application examples (llama-cpp-test, pytorch-test, faiss-test, cutlass) run only threadhist or a launch counter. Each requires rebuilding the application with PTX: PyTorch with TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST=6.1+PTX, FAISS with CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=61, CUTLASS from source.

On JetPack 7.2 the supported PyTorch path is upstream cu132 aarch64 wheels (pip index download.pytorch.org/whl/cu132). Their aarch64 CUDA 13.x arch list is Ampere 8.0, Hopper 9.0 and Blackwell 10.0/11.0/12.0. TensorRT Edge-LLM officially supports Jetson Orin on JetPack 7.2, CUDA 13.2, SM87, FP16/INT8/INT4 only.

Answer to the advisor's question, from what was gathered. The operations behind both directions are frequent in real applications only when tools run per thread: one RoPE kernel at pp512 gives 23M per-thread probe executions per prefill. The workloads bpftime can actually see on the Orin are the app-own kernels of PTX-built applications (llama.cpp quantized inference is the best case: its hot kernels are its own). PyTorch/cuDNN/cuBLAS-heavy workloads (45-76% GEMM kernel time on Orin) are mostly invisible. The 'share in real applications' question is therefore answerable on the Orin mainly for llama.cpp, FAISS's own kernels, CUTLASS and Rodinia.

gaps: Unmeasured on any source read: total kernel launches per token and the grid/block size of every kernel for llama.cpp, on the Orin or elsewhere. Measure with nsys (cuda_gpu_trace: launch count, grid x block per kernel) on TinyLlama-1.1B or Llama-3.2-1B Q4_K_M for pp512 and tg128, with and without CUDA graphs. Nothing was run on the GPU in this survey.

Untested: whether dev's driver-level hooks see cuBLAS/cuDNN/TensorRT fatbin loads at all. These libraries carry a static cudart that may fetch driver entry points through cuGetProcAddress. Also untested: the late path's (fallback that patches copies after CUDA is initialised) retargeting of sm_120 PTX to sm_87 via rewrite_ptx_target, which could compile or fail per kernel.
Untested: llama.cpp with its default-on CUDA graphs (stream capture) under dev's load substitution. gpu_ext disabled graphs (GGML_CUDA_DISABLE_GRAPHS=1).

Unverified: PTX content of the PyTorch cu132 aarch64 wheel (libtorch_cuda.so). Check with cuobjdump --list-ptx after downloading the wheel, a multi-GB download not done here. The x86 CUDA 13.0 list ending in 12.0+PTX (PyTorch PR #163585) was seen only in a search snippet.

Unknown: where TensorRT engine kernels come from at inference time. The builder-resource libraries are not fatbins to cuobjdump ('does not contain device code'). cuFFT 12.2 shows a single sm_75 cubin even with -all (likely LTO/JIT kernels). cuDNN runtime-compiled engines (NVRTC) were not traced.
Unverified for JetPack 7.2 / CUDA 13 on Orin: availability of vLLM and Triton. vLLM's per-token launch counts and kernel mix were not fetched.

Search-snippet-only numbers, deliberately not used as findings: Fleet (arXiv 2604.15379) about 250 launches per decode token over 36 layers; a blog's about 466 launches per token for vLLM eager Qwen3; lm-Meter (arXiv 2510.06126) 60% GEMM and 21% idle; arXiv 2512.01644 top-5 kernels over 90% of prefill time; ValueExpert workloads (PyTorch, Darknet, LAMMPS, Castro); the DGL cuSPARSE-vs-own-kernel dispatch; the Accel-Sim ISCA'20 workload list and its 'DeepBench closed-source kernels with no virtual ISA' sentence. The PDF read was PKA (MICRO'21), not Accel-Sim.

Not gathered: Rodinia per-application kernel counts and grid sizes beyond PKA Table 3's examples. GGUF sizes beyond TinyLlama (Llama-3.2-1B/3B, Qwen2.5-1.5B Q4_K_M). Grid sizes of FAISS, GNN and CUTLASS kernels.

Not Orin-specific: the only llama.cpp kernel-family shares (Chalmers Tables 5.1-5.2) are on H100, and the thesis says its Orin kernel analysis is less detailed. The only sm_87 kernel-time breakdown (ICDCS'26) is from PyTorch, not llama.cpp.

Still open for the advisor's question: the fraction of a real application's runtime or launches that a direction-1 or direction-2 tool would touch depends on which kernels are probed. No surveyed paper reports per-application probe-invocation counts except gpu_ext's single RoPE kernel (44 launches x 524,288 threads at pp512).
Neutrino Fig. 12's numeric values (probe memory vs model memory) were not extracted from the figure; only the text statement was read.
gpu_ext arXiv HTML was read in one summarised fetch, covering 100k of 111k characters; table and section numbers come from that fetch, not a full read.

checked.correction: (1) The 44 launches are not 22 x (Q,K). The probed symbol rope_norm<true,false,float,half> is the K-only rope: nr = PP x 4 KV heads, and TinyLlama's Q has 32 heads, so Q is a different launch shape. llama-bench by default runs a full n_prompt warm-up before the timed reps, and gpu_ext uses -r 1. Use at run time is the -fa flag, whose current llama-bench default is 'auto'; gpu_ext also passes -DGGML_CUDA_FA=ON explicitly. (4) cuBLAS is also used when should_use_mmq returns false (< 48 KiB shared memory per block), and for KQ/KQV matmuls on an F16 KV cache when FA is off [inferred]. Chalmers Table 5.1/5.2 numbers, the 4 x pp x 256 geometry and graphs defaulting ON (top-level CMakeLists sets GGML_CUDA_GRAPHS_DEFAULT ON) are confirmed.

# GPU eBPF in real applications: scenarios, workloads, and how to measure the two directions' share (2026-11-13)

The advisor asked two questions:
- Which mainstream usage scenarios exist for running code inside GPU kernels?
- In real applications, not microbenchmarks, how large a share do the operations of direction 1 and direction 2 take?

This report merges two verified surveys and proposes one measurement round on the Orin to answer the second question.

**Nothing in this report is a measured share.** None of the sources we read measures one. Every volume below is arithmetic from published launch geometry and is marked [inferred].

How the verifier results are used:
- Where a verifier corrected or struck a claim, the corrected version is used.
- The workloads verifier's output reached us cut off partway through the Chalmers item. Section 5 lists the claims that therefore have no verdict.

## Terms used in this report

**Probes and launches**
- **Probe**: an eBPF program that bpftime patches into a GPU kernel. It runs at one of three places ([PASS]):
  - kernel entry (kprobe);
  - kernel exit (kretprobe);
  - after matched load/store lines (`kprobe/__memcapture`).
  Each program attaches to one exact kernel name ([CORE] core.cpp:317-345, `m[2] == kernel`).
- **Firing**: one GPU thread running a probe once.
- **Thread execution**: one thread of one kernel launch. A launch of 524,288 threads gives 524,288 thread executions.

**Operation classes**
- **D1 op (direction 1)**: a read or write on a map whose storage is indexed by the logical thread id and sized when the map is created. In bpftime these maps are:
  - the 1502 and 1512 per-thread arrays;
  - the 1527 GPU ring buffer, which has one ring per thread.

  Other tools have fixed-size per-warp buffers with the same capacity problem; they are listed under D1 too.
- **D2 op (direction 2)**: a helper call that today makes a synchronous GPU-to-CPU round trip. These are CPU HASH maps, GPU_HASH 1501, printk and puts ([CS] class table, [CS-sum]). On the Orin each costs about 10 us, and the calls of different threads run one after another ([PROTO] 36-41).
- **Neither**: GPU-local operations: the GPU arrays 1503, 1504 and 1513, the ordinary ARRAY in dev, and the index and time helpers ([CS] class table).

**Shares**
- **Operation share**: of the map and helper operations a tool executes, the fraction that are D1, D2 or neither. Each call site is counted per firing, then multiplied by the number of firings.
- **Cost share**: the part of a tool's slowdown (time) or extra memory that comes from D1 or D2 operations.
- **Coverage**: the fraction of an application's GPU time, or of its launches, that falls in kernels bpftime can patch.

**Kernels and tools**
- **Attachable**: a kernel whose fatbin carries PTX for compute capability 8.7 or lower, and whose load passes through a bpftime hook ([NVA] 2245-2293, 488-534).
- **Own kernels**: kernels compiled from the application's source, for example llama.cpp's `mul_mat_q`.
- **Vendor kernels**: kernels that ship precompiled in NVIDIA libraries (cuBLAS, cuDNN).
- **Tool port**: a change to a bpftime tool, never to the target application. Examples: the tool's `SEC` kernel name, its map types, a thread guard. Building the application with a PTX flag is build configuration, not a rewrite.
- **CPU-style tool**: a tool written the way one writes it for the CPU, with HASH maps and printk. bpftime's cuda-counter and threadscheduling are examples.

**Labels**
- **Tier A/B/C**: the groups used to rank scenarios in section 1.
- **S1-S10**: the scenarios.
- **W1-W6**: the workloads.
- **M1-M21**: the rows of the matrix.

## Short answer so far

1. **No real-application share has been measured.**
   - Our call-site survey is static.
   - gpu_ext and Neutrino report launch geometry and overheads, not operation shares per scenario ([CS] Limits; scenarios survey, gaps).
   - The only cost share we have comes from a microbenchmark. There, host calls are about 91-97% of cuda-counter's overhead on a 32-thread vectorAdd: 320 calls per launch x 9.8-10.4 us against 3,446 us of overhead [inferred arithmetic from [RD] numbers table and [CMP] line 75].
2. **Direction 1 operations appear in real use, whatever style the tool is written in.**
   - Five of the ten scenarios keep per-thread or per-warp storage: S1, S3, S5, S7, and S4 in the form bpftime has to use.
   - Every mainstream tool sizes that storage in advance and handles overflow its own way (see S7 and S5 in section 1).
   - The one real-application measurement is gpu_ext on llama.cpp's RoPE kernel at pp512 (a 512-token prompt), on an RTX 5090. A per-thread ring of 892 MiB held 22 MiB of records, and throughput fell 90.7%. A GPU-local array holding the same 720,896 records cost 5.6% ([GX-notes] 4-8, 20-28; [GX-5090] 1-14).
   - The RoPE kernel's thread count grows 16x from a 32-token to a 512-token prompt, so any fixed capacity either loses records or wastes memory ([GX-pre] 3-18).
   - The 90.7% vs 5.6% attribution is partly [inferred]: gpu_ext did not separate the ring's size from its write path.
3. **Direction 2 operations appear only when tools are written CPU-style.**
   - No mainstream tool we read makes a synchronous host call per event. The exception is hang debugging (CUTracer `--channel-records 1`, which needs SM90 or newer) ([CUT] readme.md:9, 99-106).
   - The tools that already run on real application kernels make no host calls: bpftime's four examples on real kernels (llama.cpp, PyTorch, FAISS, CUTLASS) and gpu_ext's 15 device-side tools ([CS] Results; scenarios verifier, "added").
   - All 59 of bpftime's host-call sites sit on vectorAdd demos or `__directly_run`.
   - When a CPU-style tool does run on a real kernel, host calls dominate. One host call per thread on RoPE at pp512 is about 11.5M calls per prefill, roughly 113-120 s per call site [inferred from [PROTO]].
   - So D2's share in real applications depends on which tools people write. It has to be measured with CPU-style tool ports.
   - The survey's selection-effect caveat stands: authors who know host calls are slow avoid them ([CS] Limits).
4. **On this Orin, coverage is limited to own kernels built with PTX.**
   - Covered: llama.cpp quantized inference, CUTLASS, FAISS's own kernels, Rodinia, and the ATen kernels of a source-built PyTorch.
   - cuBLAS and cuDNN cannot be patched here: they carry PTX only for sm_120/sm_121 ([CUOBJ]; [NVA] 2245-2263). They run 45-76% of GPU kernel time in PyTorch LLM inference on Orin ([ICDCS] §V Fig. 9).
   - Triton cubins cannot be patched either. They are loaded through `cuModuleLoadData`, which dev does not hook ([TRITON] driver.c:316; [NVA] 488-534).
5. **The most common mainstream scenarios are mostly not expressible in bpftime today.**
   - S8 (correctness checking), S6 (instruction mix), S7 (region timing) and S5 (address traces) need PTX pass work: a per-instruction attach point, or the effective address as an argument ([PASS]; [MEMCAP] 45-147).
   - Today's bpftime can measure S1, S2, S3, S9 and S10 in full, and S4 only partly.
   - For S5-S8 the plan projects volumes from Nsight Compute counts.

## 2. Real workloads worth measuring on this Orin

**W1 llama.cpp, GGUF Q4_K_M (TinyLlama-1.1B; Llama-3.2-1B as a second model). Priority: first.**
- **Why it matters:**
  - It is the only real application on which device-side eBPF has been evaluated (gpu_ext) ([GX-paper] §6.4.2).
  - On sm_87, quantized matmuls run in llama.cpp's own MMQ kernels ([LCPP] mmq.cu `ggml_cuda_should_use_mmq`).
  - In Q4_K_M decode, the mul_mat_vec_q family takes 75.5% of kernel time, measured on an H100 ([CHAL] Table 5.2).
- **Attachable here:** MMQ, mul_mat_vec_q, flash_attn_ext, RoPE, rms_norm, softmax and the other own kernels. This needs a PTX build: `-DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=87`, which gives real and virtual code, or `GGML_NATIVE=OFF`, which includes 80-virtual ([LCPP] CMakeLists; CMake docs).
- **Not attachable here:** the cuBLAS path, used for F16/BF16/F32 weights or with `GGML_CUDA_FORCE_CUBLAS` ([LCPP] build.md).
- **Feasibility and caveats:**
  - The default build is not attachable. CMake expands `native` to `87-real`, which is SASS only (/usr/share/cmake-3.28/Modules/Internal/CMakeCUDAArchitecturesNative.cmake:35; [ENV] fatbin.list.txt:5-8).
  - CUDA graphs are on by default. gpu_ext set `GGML_CUDA_DISABLE_GRAPHS=1`; graphs are untested with dev ([GX-readme] 46-55).
  - The model file is 0.67 GB, with 3.17 GB maximum RAM.
  - The RoPE kernel that gpu_ext probed launches 4 x pp x 256 threads, where pp is the prompt length in tokens: 524,288 threads at pp512. It runs 22 launches per prefill. The 44 launches gpu_ext counted are a warm-up pass plus one timed pass [inferred by the verifier from llama-bench defaults] ([GX-pre]; run_table1_perf.py:71-84).

**W2 CUTLASS GEMM. Priority: second, as a control.**
- **Why it matters:** the templates compile into the application, so all kernels are its own. It is Neutrino's main GEMM workload ([NEU] Table 3), and a bpftime example exists.
- **Attachable here:** all kernels, with an sm_87 PTX build ([ENV] fatbin.list.txt:9-12).
- **Feasibility and caveats:** easy. It is a kernel benchmark, not an application, and the bpftime example is SIMT FP32, so it uses no tensor cores (example/gpu/cutlass/README.md).

**W3 FAISS IVF on SIFT1M. Priority: third.**
- **Why it matters:** vector search is a real application outside LLMs, and bpftime's faiss-test example exists.
- **Attachable here:** FAISS's own kernels: k-select, the IVF list scan and l2Norm ([FAISS] §4.2, §5.1, §5.3).
- **Not attachable here:** the distance GEMM, which runs in cuBLAS.
- **Feasibility:** a source build with the GPU enabled. SIFT1M is 1M x 128 floats, 512 MB [arithmetic], which fits.

**W4 Rodinia / Polybench. Priority: optional.**
- **Why it matters:** many small launches with different grids. Gaussian has 414 kernels and gramschmidt 6,411 ([PKA] Table 3).
- **Attachable here:** all kernels.
- **Feasibility and caveats:** trivial to build. Its inputs are sized for simulators and run in under 1 ms on real hardware ([PKA] §5.2.1), so it is weak as a real application. It is useful only as a D1 control with many kernels.

**W5 PyTorch eager (small Hugging Face Transformers LLMs). Priority: defer.**
- **Why it matters:** the mainstream framework. ICDCS'26 measured its kernel mix on Orin.
- **Attachable here:** only the ATen kernels, and only from a source build with `TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST=8.7+PTX`.
- **Not attachable here:** the GEMMs: 76.0% of kernel time for Qwen-1.5B on Orin NX, 67.5% on AGX Orin, and 44.8% for Gemma-2B ([ICDCS] Fig. 9). The pip cu132 wheels target 8.0, 9.0, 10.0, 11.0 and 12.0 ([FORUM]; dev-discuss); their PTX content was not checked.
- **Feasibility:** the wheel runs, using sm_80 SASS. A source build on an 8 GB board is heavy [inferred]. Neutrino too needed `torch.compile` to reach GEMMs ([NEU] artifact notebook, via the workloads verifier).

**W6 TensorRT / TensorRT Edge-LLM. Priority: a cheap attach check only.**
- **Why it matters:** it is NVIDIA's supported path for LLMs on Orin.
- **Attachable here:** unknown. libnvinfer has 85 PTX entries at or below sm_86 and 55 sm_87 cubins, and it does not link cudart ([CUOBJ]; `readelf -d`).
- **Not attachable here:** probably the engine kernels, but where they come from at inference time is unknown. The builder-resource libraries "do not contain device code" to cuobjdump.
- **Feasibility:** installed; attaching is untested.

**What cannot be done on this Orin, and what it would need:**
- **Vendor-library kernels (cuBLAS, cuBLASLt, cuDNN).** Their PTX targets only sm_120/sm_121 in this toolkit. On an sm_120 GPU (RTX 5090 class), bpftime's `pick_patched_ptx` would accept sm_120 PTX [inferred from [NVA] 2245-2263]. This rests on two unchecked points: the x86 libraries' PTX was not checked, and these libraries do not link libcudart, so it is untested whether dev's driver-level hooks see their loads at all.
- **Large models and serving.** Examples are vLLM with 30B MoE models, gpu_ext's GPT-OSS-120B runs (host-side policies), and 8B BF16 models. These need a discrete GPU. 8 GB of unified memory fits roughly 1-3B quantized models [inferred].
- **Hopper and Blackwell kernels, where S7 matters most.** FA3, warp-specialized GEMM, and CUTracer all need SM90 or newer.
- **Triton, TorchInductor and vLLM kernels.** No machine helps: bpftime first has to hook `cuModuleLoadData*`. That is a bpftime change, not a target rewrite ([NVA] 530-534; candidate CLAUDE.md:2146-2147, cited by the verifier).
- **Collisions between concurrent kernels.** Two processes could be run here in principle, but gpu_ext's two-tenant runs were host-side policies on larger GPUs ([GX-paper] §6.3.2).

## 4. Measurement plan for the next step

**What it answers.** For each measured cell there are four numbers:
- **Q1, coverage.** What share of the application's GPU time and launches is attachable?
- **Q2, operation share.** How many executions per call site fall in each direction, per prefill or token and per second?
- **Q3, cost share.** What part of the tool's slowdown comes from host calls? What part of its extra memory sits in thread-indexed maps?
- **Q4, D1 symptoms.** How do capacity and use compare, and how many records are lost?

**Cells.**
- Main: M1, M2, M3, M4 and M9 on llama.cpp.
- For generality: M11 and M12 (FAISS, CUTLASS); M13 is optional.
- M5-M8 are projected from Step 0 counts only, not measured with bpftime.
- M10 is left out: S10 changes behaviour, so it does not measure a share.

**Step 0: census of the application, without bpftime (the denominator)**
1. Build llama.cpp with `-DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=87` and `-DGGML_CUDA_FA=ON`, the latter as gpu_ext did. Check with `cuobjdump --list-ptx` that compute_87 PTX is present.
2. Run `llama-bench` on TinyLlama Q4_K_M:
   - prefill: `-p 32`, `-p 128` and `-p 512` with `-n 0`;
   - decode: `-p 0 -n 128`;
   - each with `GGML_CUDA_DISABLE_GRAPHS=1`, and again with graphs on.
3. Run `nsys profile -t cuda`. It gives, per kernel, the launch count, grid x block (threads per launch) and GPU time. From these:
   - thread executions per prefill and per token, for each kernel;
   - Q1: the time share of own kernels versus cuBLAS.
4. Optionally, on the top five kernels, collect Nsight Compute sass_ metrics: executed instructions, and global load and store instructions. These project the volumes of S4, S5 and S6.
5. Statically, dump llama.cpp's PTX (`cuobjdump -ptx`) and count which ld/st lines the memcapture regex matches, using `python3 -I`. This gives S4's coverage.
6. Two parts are unverified:
   - `nsys` and `ncu` are present at /usr/local/cuda/bin, but whether kernel tracing and SASS metrics work on this Tegra is unknown.
   - If they do not, a CPU uprobe on `cuLaunchKernel`/`cudaLaunchKernel` that reads the grid and block arguments can replace the census.

**Step 1: tools as written, on real kernels (D1 and the probe floor)**
1. Tools: kernelretsnoop, kernel_trace, threadhist, and mem_trace.
   - Generate one program per target kernel, from the exact mangled names, for the top kernels by time in Step 0.
   - This per-kernel generation is a tool port and is untested.
2. Count executions per call site in two ways:
   - from geometry: threads x launches x firings per thread;
   - from a counting variant of each tool, with one atomic 1503 counter per site, as a check.
3. D1 measures:
   - the configured `max_thread_count` against the largest thread count per launch among the probed kernels;
   - 1502 slots touched (non-zero) against slots allocated;
   - 1527 bytes allocated against bytes delivered;
   - records lost, computed as expected minus received. A 1527 output past the capacity returns 1 and is not counted in `dropped` ([TRAMP] 425-442).
4. Keep one fixed capacity across pp32, pp128 and pp512. This shows directly how loss and waste change with prompt length.
5. Time: tool throughput against baseline, plus an empty-probe variant (entry and exit programs with no helpers), which measures the patching floor.

**Step 2: CPU-style ports, on the same kernels (D2)**
1. Tools:
   - cuda-counter: HASH maps plus printk, about 10 host calls per thread;
   - threadscheduling: 5 host calls per thread;
   - launchlate as written: 1 printk per thread.
2. Bound every run. One per-thread call site at pp512 on RoPE takes about 113-120 s per prefill [inferred].
   - Use pp32: 720,896 thread executions per prefill, about 7 s per site and about 70 s for cuda-counter [inferred].
   - Use decode, whose kernels are small.
   - Put a total timeout on every run.
3. Count host calls:
   - with a per-helper counter in the CPU-side host-call handler (a measurement-only patch to bpftime);
   - otherwise by deriving them from geometry x per-site frequency.
4. Report host calls per second against the ceiling of about 102,000 per second [inferred].
5. Attribute the slowdown three ways:
   - (a) host calls x the measured per-call cost (9.8-10.4 us for warps, 15.6 us for a single thread; [PROTO] 36-41), divided by tool time minus baseline time;
   - (b) the same tool with each D2 site made GPU-local (HASH replaced by 1503, printk removed), which is the "eliminate/defer" form from [CS]; the time difference is the host-call share;
   - (c) the empty probe from Step 1, which gives the floor.
6. Report (a) and (b) per site class: eliminate, defer, printk.
7. Repeat with three frequency variants of each tool: as written (per thread), a warp-leader guard, and a thread-0 guard. This shows how a site's frequency class changes D2's cost.

**Step 3: generality (other workloads)**
- Run Steps 1-2 for S1 and S3 on CUTLASS (the example exists) and on FAISS IVF with SIFT1M, with the same fixed-capacity protocol.
- Optionally, run Rodinia gaussian and gramschmidt for the many-launch D1 case.
- TensorRT: one check of whether dev sees libnvinfer's modules. No measurement.

**Output: one table row per cell, with these columns**
- probed kernels and their share of application GPU time;
- firings per prefill or token;
- D1, D2 and neither operations;
- host calls per second;
- slowdown;
- host-call share of the slowdown, by (a) and by (b);

## 5. Open questions and what this survey could not establish

1. **No measured share exists.** All volumes are geometry arithmetic from one real kernel: llama.cpp RoPE, from gpu_ext's runs on other GPUs.
2. **How common each scenario is** in real use has no statistics. The ranking counts tools, and no always-on production use of in-kernel probes was found.
3. **The time split between own and vendor kernels for llama.cpp on the Orin** is unknown. Chalmers measured on an H100, and ICDCS'26 used PyTorch.
4. **Hooks on vendor libraries are untested.** It is unknown whether dev's driver-level hooks see cuBLAS, cuDNN or TensorRT loads; these libraries do not link libcudart. It is also untested whether the late path's retargeting of sm_120 PTX to sm_87 compiles.
5. **llama.cpp with its default CUDA graphs under dev** is untested.
6. **The share of llama.cpp ld/st PTX lines that the memcapture regex matches** has not been counted.
7. **nsys and ncu kernel tracing on this Tegra** is unverified.
8. **D2 depends on which tools exist.** There is no collection of CPU-style GPU tools beyond bpftime's examples. GPU ports of libbpf-tools patterns (entry/exit pairs, histograms, counters) would be the next test of whether real tools need synchronous answers.
9. **Two figures rest on inference:**
   - The 44 launches in gpu_ext are warm-up plus one timed pass; this was inferred by the verifier from llama-bench defaults.
   - gpu_ext's 90.7% vs 5.6% does not separate the ring's size from its write path.
10. **Claims whose verifier verdict was not received** (the workloads verifier output is cut off). Other items from the workloads survey were re-checked by the row verifiers (cuBLAS/cuDNN PTX, `pick_patched_ptx`, the MMQ rule, TaxBreak, PASTA, PKA, FAISS, CUTLASS, Neutrino) or by the scenarios verifier. These four were not:
    - the PTX counts of cuRAND and cuSOLVER;
    - that cuBLAS, cuBLASLt and cuDNN do not link libcudart (libnvinfer's was checked);
    - NVIDIA's forum statement that Orin runs sm_80 SASS without JIT;

11. **Sources read only through summaries:**
    - WebFetch summaries, not verbatim: KPerfIR, Proton, IKET, Triton-distributed, Compute Sanitizer and the Sanitizer API guide, the Nsight Compute guide, eGPU, gpu_ext arXiv v2.
    - Search snippets only: GPU-FPX details, the FlashInfer profiler, CUPTI SASS details, CUDA printf FIFO behaviour.
    - Re-check their numbers against the PDFs before citing them in a paper.
12. **Values not extracted:** Neutrino Fig. 12 (probe memory against model memory). Grid sizes of FAISS, CUTLASS and llama.cpp decode kernels.
13. **The papers contradict themselves:**
